newsitem.title: USA: NYC wants rent rules as prices could soar - reports.
newsitem.headline: NYC wants rent rules as prices could soar - reports.

text.p: New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani will intensify his campaign to keep rent controls, making several lobbying trips to Albany and serving as keynote speaker at Tenant Lobby Day, the New York Times said Friday.

The mayor who has been criticized for not doing enough to keep the rules, which mainly affect New York City apartments, will join City Council Speaker Peter Vallone for a lobbying trip to Albany within 10 days, the paper said.
Tenant Lobby Day is on May 20, and the rent law campaign manager for the New York State Tenants and Neighbors Coalition told the New York Times the mayor's presence would lend the event more weight.

The New York Daily News, in its Friday edition, said a new study by a major landlord group showed that tenants in the city would face sharply higher rents if controls were scrapped, estimating that tenants as a whole would pay $1.2 billion more in rent hikes each year.
On Manhattan's upper West Side, tenants in rent-stabilized apartments would see the biggest rises, with an average monthly rent hike of 51 percent.

Residents of many other neighborhoods would see their rent climb $100 or more, including 30 percent rises each month on the upper East Side and Greenwich Village, and almost 18 percent more in midtown, according to the report by the Rent Stabilization Association, a group of 25,000 city landlords. In Jamaica, Queens, average rents would rise nearly 20 percent to $677 a month, the study said, according to the News.
The average increase on a citywide basis would be 14.6 percent, said the study, which was used computer projections prepared by the American Economics Group, a Washington-based consulting firm.

And within five years, rents would soar to "stratospheric heights," the paper said. On June 15, the rent rules expire, and Senate Majority Leader Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, vowed to let that happen unless Gov George Pataki and other state leaders compromise on a two-year phaseout, the paper said.

It added that the report predicted changing to a free-market system would produce $5.3 billion in economic activity as landlords repaired neglected apartments. That would generate $563 million a year in new tax revenues, and also help create 66,528 jobs.
